The record:
Write the postmortem for the incident below.

Alert: HighLatency on io-shop
What the alert said [AL1]: p95 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}
Alert raised: 2026-11-11T02:27:15Z {alert_raised}
Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one. An alert rule fires; a person is paged. Argus first posted about the incident in Slack at 2026-11-11T02:27:40Z {first_told}, and the document says so already: leave that post out, and do not say that no person was told. That nobody was paged is a finding of its own.
The alert rule waits 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding before it fires. The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds {accounted_for} accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes {rule_waits} with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute {rule_evaluated_every}, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds {scraping_allowance} for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
Broken from 2026-11-11T02:21:00Z {began} (the onset) to 2026-11-11T02:29:00Z {back_to_normal}, when the metrics show it back to normal.
That is 8 minutes {duration}, and every impact figure below is measured over that stretch.
Argus held the incident for 3 minutes 34 seconds {held}, until 2026-11-11T02:31:10Z {argus_stopped}. That is not how long the fault lasted, nor how long Argus went on working - leave it out of your answer.
The service's error rate over all its requests, before it began: 1.1% {errors_before}.
The same rate while it was broken: 1.1% {errors_while_broken}, peaking at 2.0% {errors_at_worst} - no higher than the worst minutes of stretches as long before it began.
Rise above baseline: none beyond its normal variation - stretches as long before it began averaged as high on their own.
The series behind the alert, `max(http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.95"}) * 1000` - its alert said "p95 latency above threshold for 5m {A1}" - which its alert rule evaluates and calls worse rising: 214.25 ms {series_before} before it began, 1461 ms {series_while_broken} on average while it was broken, and 1724 ms {series_at_worst} at its worst. Say what it measures in words, not by its query.
No rise in failed requests was measured, so the harm to report is what this series did: say what it meant for the people using the service, not that little or nothing failed.
Customer loss: none - the shop's takings over the incident fell short of the same hours whole weeks earlier by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all.

What Argus did, in order:
  - [T1] 2026-11-11T02:27:35Z {T1.1} Argus: Received HighLatency on io-shop
  - [T2] 2026-11-11T02:27:50Z {T2.1} Argus: Moved the incident to INVESTIGATING - a worker took the incident up
  - [T3] 2026-11-11T02:27:50Z {T3.1} Argus: Called in the Investigator Agent
  - [T4] 2026-11-11T02:27:56Z {T4.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's per-minute metrics, anchored on 02:27:15 {T4.2}
  - [T5] 2026-11-11T02:28:01Z {T5.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 360 {T5.2} minutes of metrics
  - [T6] 2026-11-11T02:28:01Z {T6.1} Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 02:21 {T6.2}
  - [T7] 2026-11-11T02:28:01Z {T7.1} Investigator Agent: Recorded where the 3 {T7.2} replicas run - all on Tesla-V100-SXM2-16GB
  - [T8] 2026-11-11T02:28:03Z {T8.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 {T8.2} day 1 {T8.3} minute before Nov 11 02:22 {T8.4}
  - [T9] 2026-11-11T02:28:04Z {T9.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 0 {T9.2} production changes
  - [T10] 2026-11-11T02:28:04Z {T10.1} Investigator Agent: Read the service register - the service calls io-pricing (internal, owned by checkout-platform), io-summary-cache (internal, owned by checkout-platform), io-pay (third-party, owned by IO Payments Ltd)
  - [T11] 2026-11-11T02:28:04Z {T11.1} Investigator Agent: Read how far the deployment had rolled out - all 3 {T11.2} replicas run one revision, which the history does not name
  - [T12] 2026-11-11T02:28:05Z {T12.1} Investigator Agent: Asked for the service's log lines, the 8 {T12.2} minutes before 02:27 {T12.3}
  - [T13] 2026-11-11T02:28:05Z {T13.1} Investigator Agent: Read back 33 {T13.2} log lines
  - [T14] 2026-11-11T02:28:06Z {T14.1} Investigator Agent: Formed 1 {T14.2} candidate cause, best first: C1
  - [T15] 2026-11-11T02:28:06Z {T15.1} Investigator Agent: Read every channel available
  - [T16] 2026-11-11T02:28:07Z {T16.1} Argus: Read the flag provider's history - 0 {T16.2} flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 {T16.3} hour before 02:28:06 {T16.4}
  - [T17] 2026-11-11T02:28:10Z {T17.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATING to act on a candidate
  - [T18] 2026-11-11T02:28:11Z {T18.1} Argus: Called in the Mitigation Agent
  - [T19] 2026-11-11T02:28:12Z {T19.1} Mitigation Agent: Restarted io-pricing, a dependency of io-shop for C1
  - [T20] 2026-11-11T02:28:20Z {T20.1} Mitigation Agent: Waiting to see whether the service is still at the incident's level, from 02:29 {T20.2} - up to 227s {T20.3}
  - [T21] 2026-11-11T02:31:10Z {T21.1} Mitigation Agent: Looked at the service - no longer at the incident's level since 02:28 {T21.2}
  - [T22] 2026-11-11T02:31:10Z {T22.1} Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
  - [T23] 2026-11-11T02:31:10Z {T23.1} Argus: Moved the incident to MITIGATED - restarted [io-pricing] and the rule that fired stopped firing
  - [T24] 2026-11-11T02:33:06Z {T24.1} Code-Fix Agent: Proposed a fix as a draft pull request - https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/532

Changes to production it read:
  - Deploys read, none came back; flags read, none came back.

Log lines it read, one per message:
  - [G46bc] ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 17 {G46bc.1} occurrences in 9 {G46bc.2} minutes, 02:19–02:27 {G46bc.3}
  - [Gbac1] WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 9 {Gbac1.1} occurrences in 9 {Gbac1.2} minutes, 02:19–02:27 {Gbac1.3}; # was 0.50% {Gbac1.4} to 2.00% {Gbac1.5}, typically 1.50% {Gbac1.6}, highest at 02:20 {Gbac1.7}
  - [G9feb] WARN io-shop: slow upstream call - pricing.io-internal.svc took 1500ms {G9feb.1} for /v1/shoppers/shopper-#-#-#/basket-total (# of 200 {G9feb.2} requests) - 7 {G9feb.3} occurrences in 7 {G9feb.4} minutes, 02:21–02:27 {G9feb.5}; /v1/shoppers/shopper-#-#-#/basket-total took 7 {G9feb.6} different values; # was 88 {G9feb.7} to 200 {G9feb.8}, typically 200 {G9feb.9}, highest at 02:22 {G9feb.10}

Candidates it considered, in the Investigator's words - name them by their labels, but cite none; what they claim is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [C1] Calls from io-shop to the internal io-pricing service (pricing.io-internal.svc, owned by checkout-platform) began taking about 1500ms {C1.1} from 2026-11-11T02:21:00Z {C1.2}. That raised p50 and p95 for the account page. io-shop itself is unchanged: no deploys, a converged rollout, and flat CPU, memory and traffic. [internal-dependency-failure, confidence 0.88 {C1.3}, confirmed]

Actions it took:
  - [M1] Restarted io-pricing for [C1] - confirmed, nothing to put back

What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault: in src/io_shop/pricing_service.py, `basket_total` called `ask(shopper_id)` inline and waited however long it took. The account page shows the basket total only as a convenience. `_the_basket_for` in src/io_shop/account_page.py already renders the page without it (`pricing_unavailable`) when `PricingServiceFailed` is raised. A slow answer, though, never failed: whatever the pricing call took was added straight onto the page's latency. When io-pricing slowed to about 1500ms {F1.1}, every account page got about 1500ms {F1.2} slower, even though the page could have been shown without that figure. Logging that the call was slow (`slow_call`) told readers where the time went but did nothing to protect the page.
      
      The change, in src/io_shop/pricing_service.py: `basket_total` now runs the call on a small module-level thread pool and waits at most `budget_ms`, which defaults to the new `PRICING_BUDGET_MS = 500`. If the call has not finished in that time, it cancels the future and raises `PricingServiceFailed`. The message names the host, the path and the budget. A call still waiting in the pool's queue is cancelled and never runs. A call already running goes on in the background, but the page does not wait for it. A call that finishes in time behaves exactly as before: its exceptions are re-raised, a missing price still raises, and a slow `took_ms` still produces the `slow_call` words. The existing tests still describe the code as written, including `test_a_slow_answer_is_still_a_price`, because their fakes return straight away and only report a large `took_ms`.
      
      src/io_shop/account_page.py is unchanged. It already catches `PricingServiceFailed` in `_the_basket_for` and renders the page with `pricing_unavailable` and `pricing_failure`. So the page still renders when io-pricing is slow, now without the basket total. With the limit in place, a slowdown at io-pricing should add at most about 500ms {F1.3} to the page and no longer pushes the page's latency up to match io-pricing's.
      
      The tests: the new tests in tests/io_shop/test_pricing_service.py use a fake service that actually blocks until the test releases it. They check two things. When the service hangs, `basket_total` raises `PricingServiceFailed` naming the host, and it returns within a bound well below the stall. A call that answers within its budget is still a price. Against the old code, the first test would wait on the stalled fake rather than return within the bound. The new test in tests/io_shop/test_account_page.py checks that a page whose pricing service hangs still renders, with its figure and card, the unavailable message and a failure naming io-pricing, within the same kind of bound.
      
      The 500ms {F1.4} limit is a judgement call (`SLOW_CALL_MS` is 200 {F1.5}), and checkout-platform may want to tune it.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'.

How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus:
  - [U1] basket_total at src/io_shop/account_page.py:183, in _the_basket_for: calls it: return basket_total(shopper_id, ask_the_pricing_service), None
  - Where [F1] says otherwise of these lines, they stand.

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Restarted io-pricing
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #532 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

The document, by field:
root_cause: In the files Code-Fix read, io-shop's account page gets the basket total by calling io-pricing inline through `basket_total`, which waits however long the call takes and sets no time limit. The page already falls back to rendering without the total when the call raises `PricingServiceFailed`, but a slow call never raises, so however long io-pricing took was added straight onto the account page's response time. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
cause_in_plain_words: The shop's account page waits for a separate pricing service to work out the shopper's basket total, and it likely has no time limit on that wait, so when the pricing service slowed down the page slowed down too, even though it could have been shown without the total.
still_at_risk: io-pricing could slow down again, and io-shop's account pages could slow down with it.
symptom: Shop pages loaded slowly for shoppers
causal_chain 1: Shoppers waited longer for io-shop's pages: the slowest requests, the ones the service's high-percentile response time tracks, took far longer than before, while failed requests stayed within their normal range. (cites AL1)
causal_chain 2: io-shop was waiting on io-pricing: from the onset, its calls to io-pricing for a shopper's basket total took about {G9feb.1} each, for most of the requests sampled each minute. (cites G9feb, under "Log lines it read, one per message"; T6, under "What Argus did, in order"; T22, under "What Argus did, in order")
causal_chain 3: A slow io-pricing answer slowed the page because the account page calls `basket_total` inline and waits for the basket total with no time limit. (cites F1, under "What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix"; U1, under "How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main by Argus")
contributing_factors 1: The HighLatency alert on io-shop paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.
contributing_factors 1 had_it_been_otherwise: An on-call person would have known about the slowdown as soon as the alert fired, and could have stepped in if restarting io-pricing had not brought the service back.
contributing_factors 2: The record shows no alert on io-pricing's own latency. The slowdown was found only by io-shop's latency alert and then worked out from io-shop's slow-upstream-call log lines.
contributing_factors 2 had_it_been_otherwise: The slowdown would have been flagged at io-pricing itself and pointed straight at its owning team, instead of having to be worked out from io-shop's symptoms.
contributing_factors 3: io-shop's existing tests of the pricing call use fakes that answer straight away and only report a large `took_ms`, so the tests never exercised a pricing service that actually hangs.
contributing_factors 3 had_it_been_otherwise: A test with a fake that blocks would have shown that the account page waits as long as io-pricing takes, so a time limit could have been added before io-pricing slowed down.
action_items 1: Route the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call page so a person is told when it fires.
action_items 2: Add a latency alert on io-pricing's basket-total endpoint, owned by checkout-platform.
action_items 3: Require every call io-shop makes to another service to have a test with a fake service that blocks, checking that the caller returns within a bound.
action_items 4: Have checkout-platform find out why io-pricing's basket-total calls slowed down from the onset until the restart.
got_lucky 1: Argus restarted io-pricing without knowing why it had slowed down, and the restart still brought the service back, which kept the slowdown short.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {T5.1} or {duration}, are figures code writes in from the row they name. They are not judged.
  - Action items propose what to do; they make no claim about the record.
  - Whether something went well, went wrong or was lucky is a judgement. Only a fact it states is judged.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
